problem.paragraph: If $$f(x) = {\sum\limits_{n = 0}^{\infty}\frac{x^{n}}{n \text{!} }}$$ and $$g(x) = {\sum\limits_{n = 0}^{\infty}{(-1)^{n}\frac{x^{n}}{n \text{!} }}},$$ find the power series of $$\frac{1}{2}\left( {f(x) + g(x)} \right)$$ and of $$\frac{1}{2}\left( {f(x) - g(x)} \right).$$

solution.paragraph: $$12(f(x)+g(x))=\sum n=0\infty x2n(2n)!12(f(x)+g(x))=\sum n=0\infty x2n(2n)!$$ and $$12(f(x)-g(x))=\sum n=0\infty x2n+1(2n+1)!.12(f(x)-g(x))=\sum n=0\infty x2n+1(2n+1)!.$$

exercises.paragraph: The following exercises explore applications of annuities.

problem.paragraph: Calculate the present values P of an annuity in which \$10,000 is to be paid out annually for a period of 20 years, assuming interest rates of $$r = 0.03,r = 0.05,$$ and $$r = 0.07.$$
Calculate the present values P of annuities in which \$9,000 is to be paid out annually perpetually, assuming interest rates of $$r = 0.03,r = 0.05$$ and $$r = 0.07.$$
Calculate the annual payouts C to be given for 20 years on annuities having present value \$100,000 assuming respective interest rates of $$r = 0.03,r = 0.05,$$ and $$r = 0.07.$$
Calculate the annual payouts C to be given perpetually on annuities having present value \$100,000 assuming respective interest rates of $$r = 0.03,r = 0.05,$$ and $$r = 0.07.$$
Suppose that an annuity has a present value $$P = 1 \text{million dollars} .$$ What interest rate r would allow for perpetual annual payouts of \$50,000?

solution.paragraph: In general, $$P=Cr.P=Cr.$$ Thus, $$r=CP=5\times 104106=0.05.r=CP=5\times 104106=0.05.$$

problem.paragraph: [T] Evaluate the power series expansion $$\ln \left( {1 + x} \right) = {\sum\limits_{n = 1}^{\infty}{(-1)^{n - 1}\frac{x^{n}}{n}}}$$ at $$x = 1$$ to show that $$\ln (2)$$ is the sum of the alternating harmonic series. Use the alternating series test to determine how many terms of the sum are needed to estimate $$\ln (2)$$ accurate to within 0.001, and find such an approximation.

[T] Subtract the infinite series of $$\ln \left( {1 - x} \right)$$ from $$\ln \left( {1 + x} \right)$$ to get a power series for $$\ln \left( \frac{1 + x}{1 - x} \right).$$ Evaluate at $$x = \frac{1}{3}.$$ What is the smallest N such that the Nth partial sum of this series approximates $$\ln (2)$$ with an error less than 0.001?

solution.paragraph: We have $$ln(1-x)=-\sum n=1\infty xnnln(1-x)=-\sum n=1\infty xnn$$ so $$ln(1+x)=\sum n=1\infty (-1)n-1xnn.ln(1+x)=\sum n=1\infty (-1)n-1xnn.$$ Thus, $$ln(1+x1-x)=\sum n=1\infty (1+(-1)n-1)xnn=2\sum n=1\infty x2n-12n-1.ln(1+x1-x)=\sum n=1\infty (1+(-1)n-1)xnn=2\sum n=1\infty x2n-12n-1.$$ When $$x=13x=13$$ we obtain $$ln(2)=2\sum n=1\infty 132n-1(2n-1).ln(2)=2\sum n=1\infty 132n-1(2n-1).$$ We have $$2\sum n=13132n-1(2n-1)=0.69300\ldots ,2\sum n=13132n-1(2n-1)=0.69300\ldots ,$$ while $$2\sum n=14132n-1(2n-1)=0.69313\ldots 2\sum n=14132n-1(2n-1)=0.69313\ldots$$ and $$ln(2)=0.69314\ldots ;ln(2)=0.69314\ldots ;$$ therefore, $$N=4.N=4.$$

[T] Given the power series expansion $$\ln \left( {1 + x} \right) = {\sum\limits_{n = 1}^{\infty}{(-1)^{n - 1}\frac{x^{n}}{n}}},$$ determine how many terms N of the sum evaluated at $$x = -1/2$$ are needed to approximate $$\ln (2)$$ accurate to within 1/1000. Evaluate the corresponding partial sum $${\sum\limits_{n = 1}^{N}{(-1)^{n - 1}\frac{x^{n}}{n}}}.$$

solution.paragraph: When $$x=-12,-ln(2)=ln(12)=-\sum n=1\infty 1n2n.x=-12,-ln(2)=ln(12)=-\sum n=1\infty 1n2n.$$ Since $$\sum n=11\infty 1n2n<\sum n=11\infty 12n=1210,\sum n=11\infty 1n2n<\sum n=11\infty 12n=1210,$$ one has $$\sum n=1101n2n=0.69306\ldots \sum n=1101n2n=0.69306\ldots$$ whereas $$ln(2)=0.69314\ldots ;ln(2)=0.69314\ldots ;$$ therefore, $$N=10.N=10.$$

problem.paragraph: [T] Given the power series expansion $$\tan^{-1}(x) = {\sum\limits_{k = 0}^{\infty}{(-1)^{k}\frac{x^{2k + 1}}{2k + 1}}},$$ use the alternating series test to determine how many terms N of the sum evaluated at $$x = 1$$ are needed to approximate $$\tan^{-1}(1) = \frac{\pi}{4}$$ accurate to within 1/1000. Evaluate the corresponding partial sum $${\sum\limits_{k = 0}^{N}{(-1)^{k}\frac{x^{2k + 1}}{2k + 1}}}.$$

[T] Recall that $$\tan^{-1}\left( \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \right) = \frac{\pi}{6}.$$ Assuming an exact value of $$\left( \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \right),$$ estimate $$\frac{\pi}{6}$$ by evaluating partial sums $$S_{N}\left( \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \right)$$ of the power series expansion $$\tan^{-1}(x) = {\sum\limits_{k = 0}^{\infty}{(-1)^{k}\frac{x^{2k + 1}}{2k + 1}}}$$ at $$x = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}.$$ What is the smallest number N such that $$6S_{N}\left( \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \right)$$ approximates π accurately to within 0.001? How many terms are needed for accuracy to within 0.00001?

solution.paragraph: $$6SN(13)=23\sum n=0N(-1)n13n(2n+1).6SN(13)=23\sum n=0N(-1)n13n(2n+1).$$ One has $$\pi -6S4(13)=0.00101\ldots \pi -6S4(13)=0.00101\ldots$$ and $$\pi -6S5(13)=0.00028\ldots \pi -6S5(13)=0.00028\ldots$$ so $$N=5N=5$$ is the smallest partial sum with accuracy to within 0.001. Also, $$\pi -6S7(13)=0.00002\ldots \pi -6S7(13)=0.00002\ldots$$ while $$\pi -6S8(13)=-0.000007\ldots \pi -6S8(13)=-0.000007\ldots$$ so $$N=8N=8$$ is the smallest N to give accuracy to within 0.00001.
